analysis.one_liner: Requires clearer, more honest nutrition labels on packaged food, including front-of-package calorie summaries and stricter rules for claims like "natural" and "whole grain."
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate committee it was sent to on the day it was introduced, without a hearing, a vote, or any cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have overhauled food labels. It would require a standard, easy-to-read nutrition summary on the front of every package, force products labeled "made with whole grain" or "wheat" to state the actual percentage of whole grains, and ban the word "natural" on foods containing artificial ingredients like high-fructose corn syrup. It would also require caffeine content on labels, group sugars and sweeteners together in ingredient lists so companies cannot hide them, and restrict misleading claims like advertising a food as free of trans fat when it is high in saturated fat. The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any cosponsors.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, especially shoppers trying to make quick, healthy choices. The bill would put a standardized nutrition symbol on the front of every package, make serving-size calorie and added-sugar percentages visible at a glance, and end marketing practices like calling a mostly-refined-flour bread "whole wheat" or a corn-syrup-sweetened product "natural." Parents and people managing diabetes, heart disease, or weight would get clearer information without needing to read fine print.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Shoppers and families reading food labels

how_it_helps.text: Requires a simple, standard front-of-package nutrition symbol showing calories and nutrients linked to public health concerns, in a consistent, prominent location across all products [S2, S3].

Requires grain products marketed as 'whole grain', 'multigrain', or 'wheat' to state the actual percentage of whole grains or whole wheat they contain, so shoppers can see when a 'wheat bread' is mostly refined flour [S2, S3].
Bars a food from being labeled 'natural' if it contains artificial ingredients, including high-fructose corn syrup and other chemically altered ingredients [S2, S3].

Requires the Nutrition Facts panel to state the percent of recommended daily calories and added sugars provided by one serving, and restricts 'trans fat-free' style claims on foods high in saturated fat [S2, S3].

Requires caffeine content labeling for any food or drink with at least 10 milligrams of caffeine per serving, and requires packages that could reasonably be eaten in one sitting to list that whole amount as the serving [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Packaged food and beverage manufacturers, who would bear the cost of redesigning labels, substantiating health claims with documentation on demand, and reformulating or changing marketing where current labels would be deemed misbranded. Some of those costs could be passed to consumers through prices.

drawbacks.text: The front-of-package rules would take effect only three years after enactment, with two more years needed for implementing regulations, delaying any consumer benefit for years [S3].

Mandatory label redesign and claim-substantiation requirements impose real compliance costs on food manufacturers, from small producers to national brands, and those costs could be passed on in prices [S3].

The bill prescribes detailed labeling design choices by statute, including font, contrast, and symbol-system principles, reducing flexibility for regulators to adapt to consumer testing as evidence develops [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for consumers are real but modest: clearer front-of-package information, honest grain and "natural" claims, and caffeine disclosure make healthy choices easier, especially for shoppers without time to parse fine print. The costs are real too: companies would redesign labels and substantiate claims, costs that could reach consumers through prices, though experience with prior nutrition labeling rules suggests these are manageable. The bill was not carefully road-tested on specific label mockups, which made industry opposition easier. On balance, the consumer gains outweigh the compliance costs, but the bill never came close to enactment, so the weighing is hypothetical.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate health committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 5, 2013 and read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day [S1, S5].
No further action was ever recorded; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in the 113th Congress [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food manufacturers keep the current labeling rules, including marketing terms like 'natural' and 'made with whole grain' that the bill would have restricted.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured its referral to the Senate HELP Committee [S1, S3].

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over food labeling
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred, never holding a hearing or markup [S5].

against.name: Food and beverage industry trade groups
against.role: Grocery manufacturers and beverage industry associations
against.what_they_did: Have historically opposed front-of-package labeling mandates and stricter marketing-claim rules, arguing they impose costs and preempt voluntary industry labeling programs.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so no partisan split ever formed; the decisive factor was committee inaction rather than a recorded vote [S4].

industries.note: The bill would force costly label redesigns, end loose 'natural' and 'made with whole grain' marketing, and require documented substantiation of health claims. Its gain to consumers comes directly at the expense of marketing flexibility.

industries.industry: Beverage and caffeine-product makers (sodas, energy drinks)
industries.note: New caffeine-content labeling requirements would apply to any product with 10 milligrams or more per serving, adding compliance costs but mostly affecting highly caffeinated drinks marketed to young consumers.
Retailers would sell under the new labels but bear little direct compliance burden, since the requirements fall on manufacturers.
